title: The Guru cherishes the Sikh
hook: satgur sikh kee karai pratipaal: the True Guru cherishes and protects the Sikh (Sukhmani 18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok of ashtpadi 18, and your line: thank the teacher. Did a thank-you reach someone who taught you? Today the first stanza turns it around: what the teacher does for the learner. Day five hundred seven.

A kid learning to ride a bike. The parent runs alongside, one hand on the back of the seat, breathing hard. The kid wobbles, yells don't let go, and the parent says I won't. And then, at some point, the parent does let go, and keeps running anyway, a few steps behind, just in case. The kid doesn't even know. They think they're doing it alone. The first stanza of the eighteenth ashtpadi is a list of ways the Guru does exactly this for the Sikh. Today: the Guru cherishes the Sikh.
screen: `ONE HAND ON THE SEAT.` → `DON'T LET GO. I WON'T.` → `STILL RUNNING, A FEW STEPS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens: satgur sikh kee karai pratipaal. The True Guru cherishes the Sikh. Pratipaal is a lovely word. It means to nurture, protect, raise up, the way a parent raises a child or a gardener tends a plant. Then the stanza goes line by line, almost like a list of a parent's jobs. In paraphrase: the Guru is always kind to the one who serves. The Guru washes away the dirt of the Sikh's bad thinking. The Guru cuts the Sikh's bonds. The Guru gives the Sikh the wealth of the Name. The Guru sets right the Sikh's life, both this world and the next. And then the last line, the tenderest: Nanak, the True Guru holds the Sikh close, like his own life. Count what's on that list. Cleaning, freeing, giving, arranging, holding. In between, the stanza gives the Sikh a part too: the Sikh speaks the Name through the Guru's word, and turns away from vice. But nowhere does the stanza make the Guru's care wait for the Sikh to ask. That's the feel of pratipaal: care that runs ahead of the request. Notice too that the stanza says this is ongoing. Not a single rescue, but a whole relationship. Sikhs today speak of meeting that care through the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat: a hymn that lands on the right day, a langar plate handed over before anyone asked. Some would say they've been held like the kid on the bike more often than they noticed. Today's word is an invitation to look for it. Not to earn. Just to see.
screen: `PRATIPAAL: TO NURTURE AND PROTECT.` · `CLEAN, FREE, GIVE, ARRANGE, HOLD.` · `CARE THAT RUNS AHEAD OF THE ASK.` · `THE HYMN, THE SANGAT, THE PLATE.` · then, large: `CHERISHED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel cared for. Sit comfortably and let yourself be supported: by the chair, the floor, the air you're breathing. Then think back to one time you were cared for before you asked: a meal left out for you, a ride offered, a word that came at the right time. Let yourself feel it again, without explaining it away. If you pray, you can feel that care as the Guru's. If not, just let it be care. The bell holds the time.
The Guru cherishes the Sikh. Satgur sikh kee karai pratipaal: care that cleans, frees, gives and holds the Sikh close, like the Guru's own life.
screen: `THE GURU CHERISHES THE SIKH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: cherished. Today, notice one moment where someone cared for you before you asked, and let yourself receive it. Day five hundred seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib read the eighteenth ashtpadi's first stanza on how the True Guru cherishes the Sikh, and Sikhs speak of meeting that care through the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat.

match.prompt: the Guru cherishes the Sikh — tap the pairs.

myth: the stanza describes the Guru's care as a single rescue
it's an ongoing relationship: cleaning, freeing, giving, holding.
pratipaal is the kind of care a parent or gardener gives
to nurture, protect and raise up.
the stanza's lines are only about what the Guru does
it alternates: the Guru cleans and frees; the Sikh speaks the Name and turns from vice.

fork.setup: you're the kid on the bike and you think you're riding alone. by the eighteenth ashtpadi's first stanza, what's true?
options: you're being held more than you notice.
you'd better ask for help first.
fork.reveal: the stanza lists care that runs ahead of the ask, ending: the True Guru holds the Sikh close, like his own life.

original.note: Gurmukhi: pratipaal, nurturing, protecting, raising up.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Guru gives orders and the Sikh obeys.
what it means: the stanza is mostly about the Guru's care for the Sikh, given without waiting to be asked.
what a scholar hears: the stanza alternates satgur and gur kaa sikh in nearly every line, and closes with jee naal samaarai, cherishing the Sikh like one's own life.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 18, stanza 1 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286)

notes: Ashtpadi 18 stanza 1 paraphrased: satgur sikh kee karai pratipaal; sevak kau gur sadaa daiaal; sikh kee gur durmat mal hirai; satgur sikh ke bandhan kaatai; satgur sikh kau naam dhan dei; satgur sikh kaa halat palat savaarai; Nanak satgur sikh kau jee naal samaarai. Confirm.
Bike image and langar example are the writer's illustrations.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the teach claimed the Guru 'notices the dirt before the Sikh does' and cuts bonds the Sikh 'didn't know was there', which the stanza doesn't say; it now notes the stanza's alternating lines (the Sikh speaks the Name, turns from vice) and says only that the care is never made to wait on asking; cut 'most of us' and 'many Sikhs would say' claims; myth item replaced.
